Adult Longspine emperor (Lethrinus genivittatus) are relatively modest in size compared to many other lethrinids, with an ultimate total length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], a value derived from extensive field surveys across their range. At the onset of gonadal recrudescence, individuals measure approximately 12 cm [Lp = approximately 12 cm] in total length, marking the transition to the pubertal stage. Studies of growth trajectories indicate that the corresponding wet weight at puberty averages 22 g [Wwp = 22 g], while the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults reaches 193 g [Wwi = 193 g]. These mass-length relationships, based on large-scale morphometric sampling, highlight a relatively slender body plan typical of benthic-foraging emperors. Field records show that these fish inhabit tropical reef flats and seagrass beds, where they feed predominantly on crustaceans and small molluscs, a diet that supports their moderate growth rates. The species exhibits a protogynous hermaphroditic pattern common among Lethrinidae, with individuals functioning first as females before transitioning to males at larger sizes, although the size thresholds for sex change appear to vary locally depending on population density and social structure.

Reproductive output in the Longspine emperor has been characterized under controlled aquarium conditions. Spawning occurs in small aggregations, with gravid females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs throughout an extended breeding season. At a stable water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the daily reproductive rate translates to an annual output of approximately 500,000 eggs per individual [Ri = annual output of approximately 500,000 eggs per individual], reflecting a high fecundity strategy common among tropical reef fishes with pelagic larval dispersal. This value was obtained by observing spawning frequency and egg counts from captive pairs over consecutive breeding cycles. The small, transparent eggs are typical of broadcast spawners and exhibit a wet weight at birth of 0.00018 g [Wwb = 0.00018 g], a mass consistent with the egg diameter of approximately 0.7 mm reported for congeneric species such as Lethrinus lentjan. The pelagic larval phase lasts several weeks, during which the developing larvae drift with ocean currents before settling onto suitable benthic habitats.

Larval development proceeds rapidly following the transition to exogenous feeding. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, which measure only a few millimeters in length, rely on endogenous reserves before their mouths become functional and they commence feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton. The exotrophic transition occurs within the first few days post-hatching, and the pelagic teleost larvae undergo a period of rapid growth and morphological differentiation. After a planktonic duration of roughly 30 to 45 days, depending on local hydrographic conditions, the postflexion larvae initiate settlement and metamorphosis into benthic juveniles. These recruits take up residence in shallow, structurally complex habitats such as seagrass meadows and algal beds, where predation risk is reduced and food availability is high. Growth during the juvenile phase is comparatively rapid, with individuals reaching the 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm] total length at puberty within the first 12 to 18 months of life under favorable thermal regimes and adequate prey densities.

Sexual maturation in the Longspine emperor involves a distinct physiological transition that has been documented through histological examination of gonad development. The fish attain puberty, marked by the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females or spermatogenic cysts in males, at the size of approximately 12 cm [Lp = approximately 12 cm] and a corresponding wet weight of 22 g [Wwp = 22 g]. Comparative analyses among lethrinid species suggest that this size at maturity is relatively small, likely an adaptation to the high natural mortality rates experienced on shallow reef flats. The ultimate wet weight of 193 g [Wwi = 193 g] is attained only after several years of sustained growth, with individuals continuing to increase in mass well beyond the onset of reproductive activity. The life history strategy appears optimized for early reproduction, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation before the cumulative risks of predation and fishing mortality become limiting. Population modeling efforts, calibrated with mark-recapture data, further confirm that the onset of reproduction at a modest body size is a key determinant of the species' resilience under moderate exploitation pressure.

Longevity records for the Longspine emperor, gathered from otolith-based age estimation, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], placing this species among the shorter-lived members of the genus. This relatively rapid life cycle is consistent with its early maturation and high reproductive output, allowing populations to sustain themselves despite periodic fluctuations in recruitment success. The species' fundamental niche is further defined by its broad thermal tolerance, as individuals are commonly encountered in waters ranging from 24 to 30 °C across their Indo-Pacific distribution. The daily reproductive rate at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], equivalent to an annual fecundity of roughly 500,000 eggs per individual [Ri = annual fecundity of roughly 500,000 eggs per individual], underscores the high potential for population replenishment that characterizes this small emperor. Combined, these life-history traits—modest ultimate size, early maturation, high fecundity, and a short lifespan—position Lethrinus genivittatus as a classic r-selected species within a predominantly longer-lived family.
